A few days ago, OpenAI accused Apple of improperly introducing new evidence in its trade secrets case. Today, Apple has fired back, similarly accusing OpenAI of exceeding what court rules permit in its response. Here are the details.

Apple argues that OpenAI went beyond merely objecting to the new evidence

In Apple’s lawsuit accusing two former employees (Chang Liu and Tang Tan), OpenAI, and io Products of misappropriating trade secrets, one part of the case involves a motion for a preliminary injunction.

In short, Apple has asked the court to issue a preliminary injunction, arguing that doing so would prevent its trade secrets from being further incorporated into OpenAI’s hardware development while the case is being litigated.

In the legal back-and-forth surrounding that motion, Apple filed a reply brief accompanied by five expert declarations. The defendants then promptly accused Apple of improperly introducing new evidence and asked the court to strike portions of the materials.

In the defendants’ opposition filings, beyond accusing Apple of introducing new evidence, OpenAI and the other defendants also filed multiple documents to counter Apple’s arguments.

Today, Apple filed a response to those objections, arguing that the defendants went beyond merely objecting to the new evidence and instead introduced their own new arguments and evidence:

Rule 7-3(d)(1) permits a party to object to new evidence in a reply brief, but also cautions that the filing “shall not include further argument on the motion.” The defendants did not respect it—applying to use their filings to re-litigate the merits of its preliminary injunction motion. For example, the defendants disputed whether Dr. Runge had a “sufficient basis to perform the analysis,” whether he adequately responded to “countervailing evidence,” and whether he had shown that certain Apple materials were not publicly available. [⋯] Arguments like these are not objections to new evidence. [⋯] (“Statements that a plaintiff’s positions lack evidentiary support or are undermined by other evidence” are not “objections to evidence.”)

Apple also took issue with a new declaration from Liu, calling it “the most egregious overreach” in the defendants’ filings:

Notably, when the defendants submitted Liu’s declaration, they said the court should only consider it alongside the Apple evidence they were challenging.

That said, Apple argues that, since the defendants have now introduced their own new arguments, the court should consider the full record rather than striking any of the evidence Apple put forward in its reply brief.

The court has set a hearing on the preliminary injunction request for October 14.
